articles.title: Art, Surveillance, and the Politics of Memory in Southeast Asia
articles.full_text:
In recent years, the region has seen a worrying rise of moral policing and restrictions on cultural expression.
Anti-junta graffiti seen during anti-coup protests in Mandalay, Myanmar, Feb.9, 2021.
Across Southeast Asia, artists and cultural rights defenders are increasingly being cast as threats – to public morality, political order and dominant narratives about gender, sexuality, identity, and belonging.
This is especially true for queer and trans artists, whose bodies, stories, and performances often challenge the boundaries that states, religious authorities, and conservative movements seek to impose. When they are surveilled or attacked, or their work is censored, the consequences touch the foundations of civic space: the right to speak, gather, remember, imagine, and contest power.
ArtsEquator’s Southeast Asia Artistic Freedom RADAR Database documents this reality across Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam. In its 2025 report, RADAR recorded 159 challenges to artistic freedom across the seven countries. The findings closely mirror those of the CIVICUS Monitor, which rated Myanmar and Vietnam as “Closed,” Cambodia, Thailand, and the Philippines as “Repressed,” and Malaysia and Indonesia as “Obstructed.”
This matters because attacks on artistic freedom often serve as warnings about the health of civic life. Where artists are censored, surveilled, attacked, or forced into silence, broader patterns of repression are already at work.
While navigating the RADAR database, I came across “moral policing” as a category of violations faced by artists and cultural rights workers. In practice, moral policing punishes artists and communities whose work challenges artificial boundaries around gender, sexuality, faith, tradition, or national identity. It does not always manifest as an outright ban or formal legal charge. More often, it takes shape through public accusations, social pressure, police scrutiny, cancelled performances, restrictions on distribution, withdrawal of support, online harassment, physical attacks, surveillance, or the destruction of artworks.
As I dug deeper, it became evident how often LGBTQ activism and artistic expression appeared in work targeted by this category. This mirrors a trend Urgent Action Fund Asia and Pacific (UAF A&P) has been recording across its learning reports: that queer, trans and LGBTQ communities across Asia and the Pacific are increasingly being targeted through legislation, political and social attacks, isolation, and reduced resources for activism.
This broader pattern of moral policing and restrictions on cultural expression is visible in specific cases. In Vietnam, RADAR recorded 22 challenges to artistic freedom in 2025, almost double the number documented in 2024. Official Dispatch 69, issued by the Ho Chi Minh City Party Committee’s Propaganda and Mass Mobilization Department in October 2025, called for stricter measures against musical activities showing signs of “deviating from the cultural standard.” Although the dispatch did not formally ban any of the named songs or artists, it triggered a chain of reactions, including the removal of music videos from YouTube by several performers.
Vietnam also saw the targeting of VietPride in 2025. Just two days before its flagship rainbow march in Ho Chi Minh City, VietPride announced the event had been cancelled due to “external reasons.” According to RADAR, at least five other VietPride-related events in the city faced last-minute cancellations or restrictions.
RADAR’s latest report notes that, in 56 percent of cases, works or creators were portrayed as having transgressed imposed boundaries of morality, traditional values or customs, gender, sexuality, or faith, and were subjected to moral policing by state and non-state agents.
“Manufactured conflicts and moral panic over minorities, migrants, and perceived threats to traditional values have put artists at the front line of state and public attacks,” says Kathy Rowland, lead researcher for RADAR.
For artists whose identities and practices already challenge dominant norms, the pressure is intensified. Serena Magiliw, a trans actor and theatre artist from the Philippines, describes how this pressure shapes both her art and her survival.
“It is sad to know that our lives are so intertwined with being policed and surveilled because we are the embodiment of resistance,” she says.
For Magiliw, the struggle is cultural, political, and deeply economic. “I perform for a living. And if I don’t have the space to do that, I won’t survive,” she said. “I can only offer my service, which is art.”
Her words show that moral policing effectively controls whose lives are allowed to be visible, whose histories can be told, and whose futures can be imagined.
Despite these threats, artists continue to persist, finding ingenious ways to build community, extend care, and sustain resilience. Their work reaches beyond survival. It preserves memory and the legacies of hard-fought struggles, reminding new generations on the frontlines of rights movements of the ground that had once been claimed.
Resistance can leave its own mark. In 2025, Filipino drag artist Pura Luka Vega was acquitted by a Manila court of charges related to a 2023 drag performance that prompted an intense backlash from religious groups. The acquittal did not erase the cost of the ordeal, but it offered a hard-won reminder that artists and communities can push back.
In these contexts, artists are often doing work traditionally associated with human rights defenders – but without the same legal, institutional, or community-led support and protection. UAF A&P has recognized this through its Shifting Narratives program, which supports artists and cultural rights workers challenging harmful narratives affecting their communities and connects artist-activists with wider networks of rights defense and community care.
Another artist working within a highly surveilled Southeast Asian state, whose name and identity are being withheld for security and confidentiality, wrote about the relevance of their group’s work in protecting historical legacies from being censored, eradicated and expunged.
“This [work] is also about preserving memory, rather than being entirely dependent on algorithms, censorship, and platform logics. And more importantly, it’s about protecting our labor,” the artist says. “When carefully written and designed work gets deleted without a trace, it’s not just frustrating; it’s one of the reasons many activists feel exhausted. For us, this is also a form of ‘memory infrastructure’ under platform authoritarianism.”
That phrase – memory infrastructure – captures something vital about the role of artists in shrinking civic spaces. In places where public narratives are controlled, archives are fragile, platforms are unpredictable, and dissent is punished, artists help communities remember. They protect stories from disappearance. They create languages for grief, resistance, longing, and survival.
Hope and community are often the only enabling conditions under which most of these artists persist and resist. Yet at a time when all trends point to growing authoritarianism and moral policing in Southeast Asia, and to shrinking tolerance for dissent and minority expressions, art and culture remain the neural systems through which communities preserve and transmit their stories and truths.
When artists are silenced, a community loses one of its ways of imagining, and insisting on, a different future.

articles.title: ASEAN Fractures Widen as Thailand Hosts Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing
articles.full_text:
A conversation with Mark Cogan of Kansai Gaidai University in Osaka.
As the people of Myanmar recently commemorated the 8888 uprising that demanded political freedom but was brutally put down in August 1988, Thailand was playing host to Min Aung Hlaing, the former general who seized power through a coup in early 2021.
This was Min Aung Hlaing’s second official visit to an ASEAN member state since military-staged elections in December and January ensured his transition to the presidency and one that widened the schisms within ASEAN, which has barred Myanmar from official summits and events amid a bloody civil war.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul broke with that line despite ASEAN protocols and potential legal issues given the International Court of Justice will soon deliver its verdict on whether Min Aung Hlaing and Myanmar’s senior generals committed a genocide against the Rohingya.
Min Aung Hlaing’s first official visit as president was to Laos in early July and his trip to Thailand came less than a week after he allowed a representative from the International Committee of the Red Cross to meet with the jailed former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who had been unsighted for many years amid concerns for her health.
Mark Cogan is an associate professor of Peace and Conflict Studies at Kansai Gaidai University in Osaka and a regular contributor to The Diplomat. He joined Luke Hunt on Beyond the Mekong to discuss the recent developments in regional politics.
That includes the moral and political questions that have divided maritime and mainland Southeast Asia, including the civil war in Myanmar, which has claimed 100,000 lives, the Code of Conduct in the South China Sea, and Thailand’s simmering border conflict with Cambodia.

articles.title: US Official Reassures Asia of Commitment, Calls for Greater Burden Sharing
articles.full_text:
Undersecretary of War Elbridge Colby told an audience in Manila that U.S. interests are “more engaged than ever in the Indo-Pacific.”
U.S. Under Secretary of War Elbridge Colby speaks at the Ananta Centre in New Delhi, India, Mar. 24, 2026.
The United States remains strongly committed to Asia but wants its partners to bear more of the burden for their own defense, a senior Pentagon official said in the Philippines yesterday.
Seeking to counter concerns about Washington’s reliability, given the capricious character of U.S. foreign policy under the second Trump administration, Undersecretary of War Elbridge Colby said that U.S. interests were “more engaged than ever in the Indo-Pacific.”
“America is definitely not disengaging from Asia,” Colby said in a speech in Manila. “We are not leaving; in fact, we are digging in to ensure a favorable balance of power where it matters most.”
Colby made the remarks at a forum in the Philippines, his first stop on a Southeast Asian tour that will also take him and Assistant Secretary of War John Noh to Indonesia, Thailand, and Cambodia. In a statement, the Department of War said that trip, which will involve meetings with senior officials in each country, “reaffirms the Department’s commitment to build a durable peace in the region through strength.”
During the trip, Colby said in his Manila speech, he intended to “deliver a clear message that is at once both realistic and perhaps bracing but also reassuring: That America’s interests are more engaged than ever in the Indo-Pacific, and that we at the Department of War are concentrated on ensuring those interests are stoutly defended.”
Colby said maintaining a favorable balance of power in the Indo-Pacific required a “posture of deterrence by denial along the First Island Chain,” the barrier of islands that stretches from Japan down to Taiwan, the Philippines, and the northern coast of Borneo.
He pointed to what he said was a growing U.S. military commitment in the region, which has involved the deployment of additional troops, ships, aircraft, and missile systems throughout the First Island Chain. Colby described this as “a formidable, resource-backed posture calibrated to actual structural realities,” contrasting it with the “hollow, merely symbolic engagement of previous decades.”
However, he said that Washington could not manage this itself, and that local partners would need to shoulder more of the burden for their defense.
“When we ask our allies and partners to step up, to invest more in their own defense, and to take responsibility for their own sovereign security, we are not signaling abandonment,” Colby said.
He added, “We are looking for partners, not protectorates.”
The Southeast Asian tour is Colby’s official trip to Southeast Asia as undersecretary of war for policy, and in some ways, it is surprising that it has taken him 18 months to do so. But the intent of yesterday’s speech speaks to an awareness within the Pentagon of the reputational damage that Washington has suffered, in particular due to its indiscriminate tariff policy and misadventure in the Middle East.
Both of these have sent economic reverberations through Asia, and undermined the policy approach preferred by Colby. A hard-nosed realist and advocate of strategic prioritization, he has long advocated a reorientation of U.S. strategic focus from the Middle East toward East Asia, with the goal of preventing China from establishing its hegemony over the region.
While Colby did not explicitly mention China in the speech, his deterrence-focused message is likely to find a receptive audience in parts of the region that face its challenge most acutely. Chief among these is the Philippines, which has recently faced a resumption of China’s maritime pressure campaign in the South China Sea. This culminated in a clash at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands on July 20, during which a Philippine sailor sustained a head injury after being struck with a baton by a China Coast Guard member.
Despite its attendant risks, most Southeast Asian governments would prefer the U.S. to maintain a strong presence in Asia, in order to act as a counterweight against China’s growing military power. But security commitments have never been the greatest shortcoming of U.S. policy in Southeast Asia. Indeed, the long-standing complaint is that this is the only thing the U.S. does consistently in the region. This has especially been the case since President Donald Trump’s first electoral victory in 2016, which marked a decisive turn toward economic protectionism and saw the U.S. withdraw from the Trans Pacific Partnership trade pact.
This and the increasingly acrimonious strategic competition with China detracted from the fundamental goals of most governments in the region: trade and economic growth. Despite some stillborn efforts by the Biden administration, such as the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework for Prosperity, these goals have been undermined by much of the agenda of Trump 2.0, in particular the tariffing of close regional partners and allies and the war in Iran, which has led to the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, through which the region gets a significant proportion of its crude oil.
While the U.S. can help maintain a stable balance of power in Asia, it remains – at least for now – an economically disruptive force on the global stage, to the detriment of its long-term standing in Southeast Asia.

articles.title: Painting Bullseyes: What Iran’s Attacks on US Bases Mean for the Indo-Pacific
articles.full_text:
The attacks in the Middle East have raised anxieties elsewhere, as residents of communities near U.S. bases the world over worry about becoming the target of external aggression.
U.S. Army Soldiers assigned to 4th battalion, 2nd Aviation Regiment, 2nd Combat Aviation Brigade, 2d Infantry Division/ROK-U.S. Combined Division, participate in a field training exercise at Camp Humphreys, South Korea, June 30, 2026.
The United States maintains the world’s largest overseas military basing presence, with as many as 750 installations in 80 countries. Most recently, U.S. bases and bases to which the U.S. military has access in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates have become the targets of Iranian attacks, in retaliation for U.S. strikes on the country. These attacks have not only resulted in the deaths of several U.S. soldiers, but have impacted local residents in proximity to the bases and pushed others to question the necessity of the U.S. bases entirely. 
Analysts have speculated about what these attacks and the subsequent damages to the bases might mean for U.S. basing in the region, including potential base closures. 
But what does Iran’s targeting of U.S. bases and the resulting destruction mean for the rest of the 80 countries that host the U.S. military? This is an especially salient question for the host countries in the Indo-Pacific, where the specter of a U.S.-China confrontation looms large and U.S. security partners in the region maintain some of the largest troop deployments in the world, with Japan and South Korea hosting the largest and third largest deployments, respectively. 
The attacks in the Middle East have raised anxieties elsewhere, as residents of communities near U.S. bases the world over worry about becoming the target of external aggression. In the wake of Iran’s attacks, for instance, some Philippine policymakers have expressed concerns that by providing the U.S. with basing access, the Philippine government is “effectively painting bullseyes on Filipino soil” vis-à-vis China. 
Such concerns are not new in the Indo-Pacific, although the events in the Middle East may make the prospects of U.S. bases serving as targets more tangible to citizens in the host countries in the region. Peace and anti-base activists have long claimed that one potential negative externality for the communities hosting U.S. bases is that the bases and the community surrounding them may be targeted by U.S. enemies or those of the host nation. 
In Okinawa, Japan, for example, peace activists have argued that the disproportionately large U.S. base presence in the prefecture would make Okinawa “the first place for an enemy to attack.” This narrative has only grown louder as tensions between the U.S. and China, particularly over the nearby Taiwan Strait, have increased. In South Korea, one of the concerns regarding the installation of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense system in 2017 was that it would make the host village of Soseong “one of the first targets of attack” if there was conflict between the U.S. and North Korea and/or China. 
Narratives that describe the U.S. bases as dangerous to the communities which host them are part of the wider non-in-my-backyard (NIMBY) phenomenon that several scholars have noted. While citizens in the countries that host U.S. bases may generally support their country’s security alliance with the U.S., they are typically more reticent to bear the burdens of the potential negative consequences of the bases by hosting them in their community. Other potential NIMBY-related consequences range from accidents and crimes related to the U.S. troop presence to environmental degradation such as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances contamination and more quotidian issues such as base-related traffic jams and noise pollution. As with the narratives claiming that hosting a U.S. military presence will make the community a potential target of an external attack, peace and anti-base activists draw attention to these potential negative externalities as well. When activists characterize the U.S. military presence in ways that are more tangible to citizens, such as these NIMBY-related issues, they tend to be more effective at rallying anti-base protests than, for example, making pacifist and nationalistic claims.
Of course, activists’ messages and even anti-U.S.-base protests do not directly translate into general public opinion about hosting U.S. military bases. The four host countries in the Indo-Pacific included in the study (Australia, Japan, the Philippines, and South Korea) were no different, with 76 percent of Filipino respondents having very or somewhat favorable attitudes (the highest of the 14 countries), 52 percent in South Korea, and 50 percent in Australia. The rate was just 34 percent in Japan, but this was still higher than the neutral and very or somewhat unfavorable attitudes among Japanese respondents. 
A larger survey conducted this year after the onset of the U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict paints perhaps a more sobering picture, with respondents in most U.S. host countries in the survey having a net negative opinion of hosting U.S. troops. However, in these same Indo-Pacific host countries, arguably the key U.S. security partners in the region, public opinion about the U.S. bases remains among the highest, with South Korea and Japan recording net 14 and net 2 positive opinions of hosting U.S. bases, respectively. Respondents in the Philippines (-2) and Australia (-18) held more positive or undecided views combined than negative ones.
Taken together these patterns reveal a few points about what is happening in the Indo-Pacific host countries regarding protests against and public opinion about U.S. military bases following the onset of the conflict in Iran and Iran’s retaliatory attacks on U.S. installations in the region. 
First, peace activists in the Indo-Pacific, and likely in other regions outside the Middle East such as Europe, will increasingly problematize the U.S. bases as “drawing a target” on the base-hosting communities. As a scholar who recently conducted fieldwork on anti-U.S.-base activism in South Korea, I heard this narrative from several activists. 
Second, this framing may be convincing to host nation citizens, as the recent attacks on the bases in the Middle East show that this threat is both credible and tangible. 
Even if this framing has become more convincing, it may not necessarily translate into more support for the withdrawal of U.S. troops in these Indo-Pacific host countries or closure of U.S. bases. This is especially true for host countries such as South Korea, Japan, the Philippines, and Australia, which have, in recent years, been more aligned with the U.S. than China, particularly on security issues and perspectives on the regional order. However, this may be a bigger concern for Indo-Pacific countries which are trying to be politically and militarily equidistant from both the U.S. and China, in the event of a militarized conflict between the two superpowers. Additionally, as relayed to me by one interviewee, it may increase public support for developing indigenous military capability, including nuclear weapons, even for long-time U.S. allies.

This is an especially salient question for the host countries in the Indo-Pacific, where the specter of a U.S.-China confrontation looms large and U.S. security partners in the region maintain some of the largest troop deployments in the world, with Japan and South Korea hosting the largest and third largest deployments, respectively.

articles.title: Air Force Ascendant: Senior PLA Leadership Changes and Their Implications
articles.full_text:
If current trends continue, the PLAAF is likely going to have a greater-than-usual presence on the next Central Military Commission.
Chinese airmen parade during a full honors arrival ceremony at the Ministry of National Defense headquarters in Beijing, China, July 12, 2000.
Amid leadership disruption caused by the purges, the reconstruction of the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) high command is underway. Recent reports by the South China Morning Post and Channel News Asia indicate that officers from the PLA Air Force (PLAAF) have recently risen to senior leadership positions, prompting renewed discussions on the significance of this development. 
At present, PLAAF officers are in charge of five Central Military Commission (CMC) departments, compared with seven headed by Army officers, making the PLAAF the second-best-represented service at the CMC level. Moreover, of the PLA’s five theater commands, PLAAF officers lead two: the Eastern and Central Theater Commands. Meanwhile, an Army lieutenant general heads the Northern Theater Command, while a Navy vice admiral leads the Southern Theater Command. The situation within the Western Theater Command is murkier. Its commander, an Army general, has been missing for many months and his PLAAF deputy appears to have taken up some of his responsibilities. 
Overall, the expanding PLAAF presence at the top of the PLA hierarchy is obvious. If current trends continue, the PLAAF is likely going to have a greater-than-usual presence on the next CMC, whose composition is expected to be confirmed at the 21st  Party Congress in 2027. This development has the potential to reshape the PLA in multiple ways, rendering an analysis of the PLAAF’s rise and its wider implications worthy. 
The PLAAF’s representation on the CMC has historically been limited. In the Xi Jinping era, only two PLAAF officers served as CMC members: PLAAF Commander Ma Xiaotian from 2012 to 2017, and Air Force General Xu Qiliang as the CMC vice chairman from 2012 to 2022. Only one PLAAF officer served as the director of a CMC department: Air Force General Xu Xueqiang, who led the Equipment Development Department from 2022 until 2026. 
However, the limited representation may have been a blessing in disguise. As officers from other services rose to prominence, many quickly became targets of the expanding purges. With few senior leaders at high posts, the PLAAF was less exposed to the turbulence. From 2013 to 2026, there were only ten documented cases of senior PLAAF officers falling victim to the purges, with the most recent cases being the aforementioned Xu Xueqiang and the PLAAF’s 14th Political Commissar Guo Puxiao. 
The survival of PLAAF officers provided Xi with a larger pool of candidates to draw upon as he seeks to rebuild the PLA’s senior leadership. Also, PLAAF officers’ ability to survive constant Discipline Inspection Commission surveillance may have strengthened Xi’s confidence in their reliability. The rise of PLAAF officers is therefore natural in a time of leadership reconstruction amid elevating global tensions, creating a situation where military talents are desperately needed.  
The rise of PLAAF officers to senior leadership posts could influence future PLA development in several ways. As PLAAF officers gain more say, they are likely to advocate for their service and specialties. At CMC meetings, they are certain to promote the importance of air power, which has proved to be critical in recent conflicts. At the beginning of the Iran War, U.S. and Israeli air superiority enabled the decapitation of Iran’s civilian and military leadership. However, vulnerabilities in U.S. and Gulf states’ air defenses subsequently shifted the initiative and drained U.S. stocks of critical interceptors. The conflict highlighted the need to invest resources to improve offensive and defensive capabilities in the air domain.
PLAAF officers could cite these examples to advocate for more investment in air defense systems, unmanned aerial vehicles, counter-drone technologies, air base protection, and munitions production. Such investments could benefit the PLA, since China’s next war will likely require extensive air force participation. The recent revelation of the air-launched, nuclear-capable JL-1 missile on board the H-6N bomber may reflect China’s intent to strengthen and expand its air force capabilities. 
A stronger emphasis on air power will divert more resources to the PLAAF. Yet, an unintended consequence might be resource competition with the traditionally powerful Army, whose personnel constitute nearly half of the PLA and occupy a majority of senior leadership posts. Xi cannot afford to alienate the Army, which remains the bedrock of the armed forces and essential to regime security. Looking ahead, Xi is likely to use his personal authority as CMC chairman to mitigate possible tensions between the ascendant airmen and still-dominant army officers, with the ultimate goal being achieving greater jointness across the services. 
As Xi constructs a new generation of PLA leaders, he seems to favor a team with a significant number of PLAAF officers. This development could benefit PLA capabilities by giving more institutional weight to air power, when its relevance to military success has been made evident through recent conflicts. Nonetheless, one should expect politics to overshadow officer selection and promotion, as this has always been the case with the PLA. 
In the Xi era, the PLA has experienced considerable instability due to the anti-corruption campaign. There is no guarantee that the now favored PLAAF officers will not fall prey to the rolling purges, despite their previous experience as the least affected service. Ultimately, the past has shown that the higher PLA officers move up in the chain of command, the greater scrutiny they face, as they become enmeshed in an environment of mistrust. In essence, one must not disregard the influence of politics when analyzing the trajectory of PLA developments.  
There may be a short period of unity among senior PLA leaders after the 21st Party Congress. However, if recurring dynamics of the Xi era endure, instability could reemerge once again to disrupt PLA capability, even undermining the careers of PLAAF officers who are currently on the ascent.

articles.title: Safeguarding Storage: Wildberries’ Move to Kazakhstan
articles.full_text:
As drone strikes on Wildberries warehouses across Russia continue, the company moves to increase its presence in Kazakhstan
On August 4, Kazakhstani Minister for Trade and Integration Arman Shakkaliyev announced that the Russian e-commerce platform Wildberries would expand its warehouse capacity in the country. According to the minister, Wildberries plans to build 260,000 square meters of storage, split between Astana and Almaty, expanding its capacity more than eightfold from its current 46,000 square meters of leased warehouse space. 
The announcement comes following a July marked by more than 20 attacks on Wildberries’ logistical hubs across Russia, also affecting Kazakh sellers on the platform who have lost an estimated $3.2 million worth of goods.
Despite media reports framing the expansion as a relocation of the e-commerce platform, the planned warehouses in Kazakhstan would not be able to cover the more than 1 million square meters lost over the last month. On top of this, Wildberries’ new warehouses planned in Kazakhstan are, at the time of writing, only set to be completed in 2027, thereby not solving the current problems facing the company. This news, however, came just days after the Russian newspaper cited multiple sources saying the company was looking for 100,000 square meters of extra storage.
Wildberries’ overall aim to build more warehouses in Kazakhstan is not new. In fact, such an effort announced at the beginning of 2023, with plans to open two years later before the project was postponed. The company’s market share in Kazakhstan has grown, now making it a distant second with almost 27 percent of the e-commerce market. Locally founded Kaspi keeps almost two-thirds of the market.
Wildberries is reportedly scrambling to find an additional 100,000 square meters of warehouse space as a result of the last month’s many attacks. Reports of this new search for space came as it became clear that losses at Wildberries hubs in Russia could amount to upward of $3.37 billion.
With losses from Kazakh vendors alone exceeding $3 million, Shakkaliyev, during the announcement of Wildberries’ construction plan, urged Kazakh citizens to use local e-commerce platforms like Kaspi rather than foreign alternatives, both for selling and buying goods.
“We must use our domestic marketplaces. We call this economic patriotism. We currently have a very high share of domestic marketplaces, so, of course, we should try to order locally,” the minister said, stating that only through these channels could people be guaranteed that their products were delivered.
This statement is just one sign that the role of Wildberries in Kazakhstan, and Central Asia in general, could be challenged by the recent attacks. Even before this advice was given, Kyrgyz clothing manufacturers showed interest in replacing Wildberries with Kazakh platforms, both due to financial interest and the protection of the stored inventory.
Likewise, Kazakh sellers have taken into consideration using local platforms from either Kazakhstan or a larger market like Uzbekistan. A central issue for some of the sellers was, however, access to the much larger Russian market.
New warehouses could become key for Wildberries going forward for reasons beyond keeping its market share. According to a Kommersant report, for example, expansion of the e-commerce company’s Kazakh operations was linked to wishes of protecting some of its goods, rather than just local expansion. By constructing warehouses in Kazakhstan and neighboring Uzbekistan, Wildberries could safeguard parts of its inventory and some of the losses it has taken over the past month.
Similar measures were taken in early August by competing Russian e-commerce platform OZON, which focused on moving expensive goods away from more easily targetable logistical hubs.
While the future opening of new logistical hubs might increase Wildberries’ importance in Kazakhstan, it does not seem likely to safeguard the company as a whole. Instead, what will be relevant is what the Russian e-commerce heavyweight decides to put in these new Central Asian warehouses and what the state of the company will be at that time.

articles.title: The Mecca Pact Extends Pakistan’s Security Role Westward
articles.full_text:
Six months ago, it was unclear whether trilateral discussions between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye would produce a formal agreement. They now have.
At the time of their exploratory trilateral talks in February, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan had no formal defense commitment. It was unclear whether the discussions would produce much beyond political coordination. That has now changed.
On August 7, the three governments signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. Its main provision stipulates that an armed attack on one party will be regarded as an attack on all three. Yet the public account of the agreement leaves the resulting military obligations undefined. There is no disclosed procedure for deciding that an attack has triggered the pact, no announced geographical limit, and no public explanation of what assistance each country must provide.
The comparison with NATO’s Article 5 is useful, but only in a limited sense. Article 5 leaves each ally discretion over the action it considers necessary. NATO also has decades of military planning and cooperation behind it. Nothing comparable has yet been publicly disclosed for the Mecca pact.
Saudi Arabia has made similar attempts before. The Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition, announced in 2015, eventually brought together 41 states under a Saudi-led structure. A former Pakistani army chief, Raheel Sharif, became its military commander. Participation still depended on each country’s own decisions, and member sovereignty was explicitly preserved. This history makes the “Muslim NATO” label for the Mecca pact premature. Mecca has far fewer members, but its mutual-defense pledge does go much further.
Pakistan has already shown what a defense commitment to Saudi Arabia can mean in practice. During the spring phase of the Iran war earlier this year, Islamabad deployed a reported 8,000 troops, JF-17 fighters, drones, and a Chinese HQ-9 air-defense system to Saudi Arabia under the bilateral 2025 Saudi-Pakistani defense agreement. Pakistani personnel operated the equipment while Saudi Arabia financed the deployment. Islamabad did not respond militarily to Iran’s attacks on Saudi Arabia and at the same time worked to mediate the Iran-U.S. conflict.
This may offer a better model for the new pact than a fully integrated alliance. Pakistan can deploy its own forces and systems without giving up control over them. Turkiye could follow a similar model. The three countries do not need to integrate all of their military systems before they can work together on specific missions.
For Pakistan, this means taking on a more formal security role in the Gulf. India remains the central reference point in Pakistani defense planning, while Afghanistan and Iran shape its western security environment. But Islamabad can now use its military capacity to gain political access, defense sales, Saudi financing, and a larger role beyond South Asia.
There are costs as well. A future India-Pakistan crisis would test how Riyadh and Ankara interpret the collective-defense clause. New Delhi has said it is closely following the pact, while Saudi Arabia has continued to maintain and develop its strategic relationship with India. Riyadh therefore has good reason to keep its Pakistan commitment from turning every India-Pakistan confrontation into a Saudi-Indian crisis.
Pakistan’s nuclear arsenal raises a separate question. Possessing nuclear weapons and extending a nuclear guarantee are different decisions. There is no public evidence that Islamabad has formally placed Turkiye or Saudi Arabia under its nuclear deterrent. Saudi officials have said the Mecca agreement is unrelated to nuclear ambitions or an arms race. Pakistan had also previously said that nuclear weapons were “not on the radar” of its Saudi defense agreement. Pakistan’s arsenal still matters because one member of the pact has escalation options that the others do not. But there is no confirmed extended nuclear guarantee.
China supplied 80 percent of Pakistan’s major arms imports in 2021-25. Saudi Arabia remains heavily tied to U.S. and other Western equipment, while Turkiye uses both NATO-standard and domestically produced systems. This will make some forms of military cooperation difficult, especially where communications, maintenance, and sensitive technology are concerned.
Pakistan’s May deployment also shows that full integration may not be necessary. Chinese-origin equipment contributed to Saudi defense through Pakistani-operated units without requiring Riyadh to reorganize its armed forces around those systems.
Riyadh is also trying to build more of its defense industry at home. Its official strategy aims to localize more than half of military spending by 2030 and lists strategic autonomy among its priorities. Saudi-Turkish cooperation already offers one example. A 2023 agreement between SAMI and Baykar covered local manufacturing, final testing, training, and support. Pakistan could become more closely involved in the same process. Saudi capital and procurement can help Turkish and Pakistani manufacturers produce at greater scale, while Riyadh can use those partnerships to build more capacity inside the kingdom.
This could also make the relationship harder to unwind when the immediate security environment changes. Long-term procurement, training, and joint production can survive political disagreements more easily than summit-level coordination alone.
At the same time, the pact is poor evidence for a post-American regional order. In January, U.S. Central Command and regional partners opened a new air- and missile-defense coordination cell at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. The Combined Air Operations Center there includes representatives from 17 countries. Saudi Arabia also deepened its bilateral defense relationship with Washington in November 2025, and Washington said that Riyadh continued to regard the United States as its primary strategic partner. American military and intelligence support remains difficult for regional powers to replace.
The Mecca pact may instead give the three countries more room to operate inside the existing system. Saudi Arabia gains more sources of military support. Turkiye gains another regional security channel that is not directly controlled by Washington. Pakistan can provide Gulf partners with forces and Chinese-origin equipment while keeping ties with both Beijing and Washington. The same arrangement can therefore look like burden-sharing from the perspective of the United States and greater flexibility from that of the three signatories.
There is a distant historical parallel. Declassified U.S. records show that Turkiye, Pakistan, and Iran pushed for a permanent CENTO command structure in 1960, while Washington resisted because of the political and financial obligations it might create. The United States was never a formal CENTO member but took part extensively in its activities. U.S. records later described Washington as an observer that participated fully.
The comparison should not be taken too far, however. The Mecca pact was negotiated by the regional states themselves, and the United States is not a party. But Saudi Arabia still depends heavily on American capabilities, Turkiye is a NATO member, and Pakistan maintains important relationships with both Washington and Beijing. The three Mecca pact countries have more room to act for themselves than they did in the CENTO era, but that does not yet amount to strategic independence.
The Red Sea may show more quickly what the pact can actually do. On July 30, Saudi Arabia proposed a multinational maritime-defense coalition for the Red Sea, Bab el-Mandeb, and the Gulf of Aden after renewed Houthi attacks. Turkiye and Pakistan were among 14 governments supporting the initiative, alongside Egypt, Sudan, and Djibouti.
This also offers a simple way for the wider network to grow. Egypt, for example, can work with the three countries in the Red Sea without accepting a collective-defense commitment involving Pakistan. Other governments can take part in particular missions or exercises when their interests overlap.
The three members will still approach crises differently. Saudi Arabia faces attacks from Iran-aligned forces and threats to its energy infrastructure. Pakistan remains focused on India and has strong reasons to keep a working relationship with Iran. Turkiye has NATO commitments and its own regional priorities. The pact will have to work around these differences.
What happens next will matter more than another summit. Regular exercises, joint planning, and clear procedures for dealing with a crisis would show that the agreement is becoming more than a political pledge.
Six months ago, it was unclear whether the trilateral discussions would produce a formal agreement. They now have. The harder question is whether three countries with different military systems, external partners, and security priorities can make that agreement credible without losing the flexibility that brought them together.
For Pakistan, the immediate result is a wider security role. Gulf and potentially Red Sea crises now sit closer to its South Asian calculations. This can raise Islamabad’s strategic value and create new economic opportunities, but it also gives Pakistan more crises to manage outside its traditional theater. Whether the Mecca pact increases Pakistan’s room for maneuver will depend on how well Islamabad handles that trade-off.
At the time of their exploratory trilateral talks in February, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan had no formal defense commitment. It was unclear whether the discussions would produce much beyond political coordination. That has now changed.
On August 7, the three governments signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. Its main provision stipulates that an armed attack on one party will be regarded as an attack on all three. Yet the public account of the agreement leaves the resulting military obligations undefined. There is no disclosed procedure for deciding that an attack has triggered the pact, no announced geographical limit, and no public explanation of what assistance each country must provide.
The comparison with NATO’s Article 5 is useful, but only in a limited sense. Article 5 leaves each ally discretion over the action it considers necessary. NATO also has decades of military planning and cooperation behind it. Nothing comparable has yet been publicly disclosed for the Mecca pact.
Saudi Arabia has made similar attempts before. The Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition, announced in 2015, eventually brought together 41 states under a Saudi-led structure. A former Pakistani army chief, Raheel Sharif, became its military commander. Participation still depended on each country’s own decisions, and member sovereignty was explicitly preserved. This history makes the “Muslim NATO” label for the Mecca pact premature. Mecca has far fewer members, but its mutual-defense pledge does go much further.
Pakistan has already shown what a defense commitment to Saudi Arabia can mean in practice. During the spring phase of the Iran war earlier this year, Islamabad deployed a reported 8,000 troops, JF-17 fighters, drones, and a Chinese HQ-9 air-defense system to Saudi Arabia under the bilateral 2025 Saudi-Pakistani defense agreement. Pakistani personnel operated the equipment while Saudi Arabia financed the deployment. Islamabad did not respond militarily to Iran’s attacks on Saudi Arabia and at the same time worked to mediate the Iran-U.S. conflict.
This may offer a better model for the new pact than a fully integrated alliance. Pakistan can deploy its own forces and systems without giving up control over them. Turkiye could follow a similar model. The three countries do not need to integrate all of their military systems before they can work together on specific missions.
articles.summary: Six months ago, it was unclear whether trilateral discussions between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye would produce a formal agreement. They now have.

articles.title: Austria Says No to the Tajik Government
articles.full_text:
In Vienna, judges have now rejected four names from Dushanbe’s 18-person extradition dossier.
A criminal court in Vienna on August 5 refused Tajikistan’s request to extradite Shavkat Muhammad, a member of the banned National Alliance of Tajikistan, along with his 77-year-old mother, Sharofat Sharifova, and his brother Bilolidin Sharifov. Tajik authorities accuse the three of extremism; the family calls the prosecution political. 
No written ruling has been published, and the account of the hearing comes from opposition figures who were in the room.
This is the fourth refusal to come out of a single Tajik submission. In April, the Interior Ministry sent Austria’s Justice Ministry files on 18 members of exiled opposition organizations, a dossier Leila Nazgul Seiitbek examined for the Diplomat in June. On June 24, a Vienna court took up the case of Islamic Renaissance Party of Tajikistan (IRPT) member Firdavs Shukurov. The conduct Dushanbe cited in its own case materials was Shukurov holding an anti-Rahmon banner at an October 2021 demonstration in Vienna, partly documented in a YouTube video. The rally had been authorized and Shukurov held refugee status. Five days later the same court blocked the return of a 49-year-old woman wanted since 2018 for public calls to change the constitutional order.
Austria has not always drawn a firm line on these kinds of requests, and the difference appears to have been procedural. In March 2020 it removed Hizbullo Shovalizoda after rejecting his asylum claim, a migration decision rather than an extradition ruling. He was detained on arrival in Dushanbe and sentenced in June to 20 years for treason and participation in an extremist organization in a closed trial. An Austrian court later invalidated the removal, finding that the asylum decision had relied on outdated information about conditions in Tajikistan, and obliged Vienna to bring him back. He is still in prison.
Elsewhere in Europe, we see similar patterns in which there is a divide between extradition requests and migration violations, regardless of the reality on the other end in Tajikistan. 
On June 20, Germany deported Asadullo Boboev, 54, and his 19-year-old son to Dushanbe. Boboev was placed in pretrial detention on arrival. A court in Geldern had authorized their pre-removal detention on the basis of expired residence status and repeated failure to leave voluntarily. Boboev had separately been given until July 1 to satisfy a German court that a criminal case awaited him, a deadline that passed while he was already in Tajik custody. His lawyer submitted dozens of pages documenting the risk of return, which the court disregarded, according to exiled opposition leader Sharofiddin Gadoev.
Human Rights Watch counts Boboev as the fourth documented Tajik opposition activist deported by Germany since 2023 and detained on landing. Abdullohi Shamsiddin, whose German case turned on a failure to register with the migration service, got seven years at home for liking a social media post; Bilol Qurbonaliev received ten and Dilmurod Ergashev eight. Poland deported Farrukh Ikromov in April 2024 after Germany returned him under the Dublin rules; family and opposition sources say a closed court gave him 23 years, a conviction Tajik authorities have never confirmed. Sweden returned Farhod Negmatov and his three underage daughters in December 2024. Negmatov was detained on landing.
The machinery behind these requests is outsized for a country of 10 million. Leaked Interpol records obtained by Disclose and the BBC placed Tajikistan third worldwide for red notices in circulation in late September 2024, ahead of China in seventh; Interpol publishes no such ranking. The Interior Ministry of Tajikistan said in July that 4,225 Tajik citizens are on the Interpol wanted list, 403 of them added since January, and that Russia handed over 373 in the first half of 2026. Neither figure is independently audited. Freedom House, which counts Tajikistan among the ten worst perpetrators of transnational repression, found that terrorism or extremism accusations appear in more than 46 percent of documented cases worldwide since 2014.

Removal puts the migrant’s own paperwork (or lack thereof) in front of a judge instead; the prohibition on returning anyone to a real risk of torture still binds, but it arrives as something the person facing deportation must establish, on a schedule the deportation sets, rather than as a case the requesting state has to make.

articles.title: The China-Russia-North Korea Authoritarian Axis Looms Over Wars in Ukraine and Iran
articles.full_text:
Taiwan and other Indo-Pacific targets could be next.
China’s reported sale of shoulder-launched missile systems to Iran should be concerning not just to the United States but also to Australia and other major powers in the Indo-Pacific.  It demonstrates a deeper strategic partnership between Beijing and Tehran – one with destabilizing consequences for the Middle East – and shows a certain recklessness in Chinese behavior.
But China is not alone in this endeavor. Russia is an active party aiding Iran in a variety of ways, even though it has its hands full with its ill-advised invasion of Ukraine. Sino-Russian assistance to Iran degrades the international security situation in the Middle East and worsens the Strait of Hormuz crisis. And North Korea is involved too, completing the authoritarian axis.
According to a July 29 Reuters report, the China-Iran weapons contract is for shoulder-fired missile systems – up to 400 QW-12 and FN-16 man-portable air defense systems – under a deal worth between $60 million and $70 million. The missile systems could help Iran rebuild short-range air defenses, which have been severely degraded after five months of Israeli-U.S. military strikes.
To hide its role, China reportedly had a Hong Kong-based company, Zhongqing Baoshang International Investment, act as a middle agent facilitating the deal with Iran. China’s Foreign Ministry rejected the reports, saying that they had “no factual ground at all.” The Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson also added that “China always works for peace and the end of the conflict.” China’s Defense Ministry spokesperson made a similar statement saying that he was “not familiar with the relevant situation.”
This isn’t the first time reports about China’s sale of missile systems have become public. In February, Reuters reported that Iran and China were closing a deal for the sale of Chinese CM-302 supersonic anti-ship missiles. With a 290 km range, these were meant to boost Iran’s strike capabilities against the U.S. navy. In April, The New York Times, citing U.S. intelligence agencies, reported that China “may have sent a shipment of shoulder-fired missiles to Iran.” However, this report was somewhat unclear, as “the intelligence is not definitive that the shipment has been sent,” nor was there clear evidence that Iran had used the missiles against the United States. Nevertheless, these repeated reports show that China has enough stake in Iran to provide military supplies, despite the risks involved.
In May, the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned 12 Chinese entities and six individuals for providing assistance to Iran for its ballistic missile program. China was thought to be providing chemical precursors and other dual-use items that went to Iran’s ballistic missile program.
Russia, too, has been arming Iran. In March, there were reports that detailed the scale of Moscow’s assistance to Tehran. This included the provision of medicine, food, drones, and intelligence, such as targeting information to help Iran hit U.S. assets in the Middle East. In September 2022, Iran supplied Shahed drones to Russia for its war in Ukraine. Now, Tehran is reportedly getting the more advanced versions of those drones from Moscow. The Financial Times reported that the “dramatically improved” version of the Shahed includes “modifications to the engines, navigation and anti-jamming capabilities.” There are also indications that the newer Russian drones come with Chinese radio modems, cameras, and a range of other improvements that make them even more difficult to counter. In addition, and drawing from its own drone warfare experience in Ukraine, Russia was also reportedly providing Iran with “tactical guidance on how many drones should be used in operations and what altitudes they should strike from.”
Completing the authoritarian axis, North Korea is reportedly gearing up to send around 30,000 troops to Russia. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on July 30 that Russia’s Voronezh region was getting ready to receive the North Korean troops. He added that North Korea was also likely sending “additional missile launchers” to further Russia’s military operations in Ukraine. Zelenskyy also said that the threat was not limited to Ukraine alone, as Russia was helping North Korea “learn how to wage war, improve its weapons and gain real combat experience ⁠in using them.” This should be concerning to other countries in the Indo-Pacific, especially Japan and South Korea.
Chinese and Russian assistance to Iran could have serious effects on Middle Eastern security dynamics, including potentially prolonging the war in Iran. Australia and other Indo-Pacific powers should be alert to deepening cooperation between authoritarian powers. These powers are already working together in Ukraine. Now they are in Iran, again trying to undermine the U.S. and its partners. Taiwan and other Indo-Pacific targets could be next.
This article was originally published in ASPI’s The Strategist.

articles.title: Samsung, SK Hynix Tests of Chinese Chip Tools Expose Cracks in US Export Strategy
articles.full_text:
South Korean chipmakers are evaluating Chinese equipment as a hedge against shifting export rules from Washington.
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the two largest global memory chipmakers, have spent roughly two years testing chipmaking equipment from the Chinese firm Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment Inc. (AMEC), according to local news reports. The trials, first reported by Reuters on August 5, amount to a hedge against tightening U.S. export controls that could eventually cut Western companies off from servicing tools already installed inside the two firms’ Chinese factories.
Samsung has denied testing AMEC equipment at its China site or considering such a test, and SK Hynix has not commented on the matter. Even so, engineers at both companies began qualifying AMEC’s etching tools around two years ago. At the time, it was unclear whether Washington would keep allowing imports of U.S. chipmaking equipment into China.
In 2023, the U.S. Commerce Department designated Samsung and SK Hynix’s Chinese factories as validated end users. The status let the companies import certain controlled American equipment without applying for a license each time. However, Washington revoked the status in 2025, then granted both firms a narrower annual license covering equipment imports for 2026. Each policy swing left the two chipmakers less certain their existing American and Dutch tools would keep receiving spare parts, software updates, and repair support. Memory-chip production lines depend on equipment calibrated with extreme precision and supplier uncertainty is difficult for a fab to absorb.
Alongside tightening U.S. export controls, China’s chipmaking industry has been making rapid strides. A state-backed manufacturer based in Shanghai began mass-producing immersion deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines in late July, aiming to deliver roughly five units this year and about 20 in 2027 to three of the country’s leading chipmakers. The manufacturer has been identified as Shanghai Aishengna Electronic Technology Group, a company built by absorbing engineering teams from several Chinese lithography startups.
Lithography machines etch the circuit patterns that give a chip its function. The technology has long been dominated by the Dutch firm ASML which builds the extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, systems needed for the most advanced chips. The Aishengna machines use DUV, an older process that falls well short of ASML’s capabilities and are not expected to pose an immediate commercial threat to the Dutch company.
China’s drive for chip-hardware self-sufficiency is now paired with a push into finished AI chips. Huawei plans to launch its Ascend 950 processors and Atlas 950 SuperPod computing system in South Korea in the fourth quarter of 2026, positioning them as a cheaper alternative to U.S. firm Nvidia’s export-compliant H20 chip. Huawei has signed distribution agreements with two Korean partners, Hansol PNS and SK Shieldus, and says its inference-focused chip delivers roughly 2.87 times the performance of Nvidia’s H20 at about a quarter of the price.
Experts point to Beijing’s approach to industrial regulation as one of its key drivers for this rapid development of cutting-edge technology. Carl Benedikt Frey, an associate professor of AI & Work at the Oxford Internet Institute and a Fellow of Mansfield College at the University of Oxford, recently argued that China’s “move fast and regulate later” strategy has spurred growth in emerging technology like artificial intelligence and renewable energy at an accelerated pace, although that strategy raises questions about the security and quality of Chinese innovations.
Security concerns about Chinese technology and doubts over software support could still slow Huawei’s adoption in South Korea, even as its AI chip launch stays on track for the fourth quarter of this year. Aishengna’s lithography output, meanwhile, is expected to grow to about 20 units in 2027. Samsung and SK Hynix have not said whether their AMEC trials will move beyond testing.

Carl Benedikt Frey, an associate professor of AI & Work at the Oxford Internet Institute and a Fellow of Mansfield College at the University of Oxford, recently argued that China’s “move fast and regulate later” strategy has spurred growth in emerging technology like artificial intelligence and renewable energy at an accelerated pace, although that strategy raises questions about the security and quality of Chinese innovations.
Security concerns about Chinese technology and doubts over software support could still slow Huawei’s adoption in South Korea, even as its AI chip launch stays on track for the fourth quarter of this year. Aishengna’s lithography output, meanwhile, is expected to grow to about 20 units in 2027. Samsung and SK Hynix have not said whether their AMEC trials will move beyond testing.
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the two largest global memory chipmakers, have spent roughly two years testing chipmaking equipment from the Chinese firm Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment Inc. (AMEC), according to local news reports. The trials, first reported by Reuters on August 5, amount to a hedge against tightening U.S. export controls that could eventually cut Western companies off from servicing tools already installed inside the two firms’ Chinese factories.
Samsung has denied testing AMEC equipment at its China site or considering such a test, and SK Hynix has not commented on the matter. Even so, engineers at both companies began qualifying AMEC’s etching tools around two years ago. At the time, it was unclear whether Washington would keep allowing imports of U.S. chipmaking equipment into China.
Mitch Shin is a chief correspondent for The Diplomat, covering the Korean Peninsula. He is also a non-resident research fellow at the Central European Institute of Asian Studies and associate fellow for the Swedish Institute of International Affairs.
articles.summary: South Korean chipmakers are evaluating Chinese equipment as a hedge against shifting export rules from Washington.

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina’s Media Event in India Hits Bangladesh-India Ties
articles.full_text:
By giving the deposed Bangladeshi PM a platform to lash out at the present regime from Indian soil, India has signaled that it still stands with its old friend.
A file photo of then-Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina with her Indian counterpart Narendra Modi during her visit to New Delhi, India, weeks before her ouster from power in 2024.
New Delhi’s decision to allow deposed Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to hold a press conference on August 5, coinciding with the second anniversary of the toppling of her government in a student uprising in 2024, has set back India’s ties with the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government in Dhaka.
What is most intriguing is the timing. Ties with the Tarique Rahman-led government were on the mend as Bangladesh Foreign Minister Dr. Khalilur Rahman visited New Delhi from April 7 to 9, marking the first high-level ministerial engagement. India too had sent an invitation to Prime Minister Rahman to attend the BRICS summit to be held in New Delhi in September. Bilateral trade and the issuing of visas to Bangladeshi citizens had resumed. The appointment of Dinesh Trivedi, a senior politician, as India’s new high commissioner was seen as a thawing of frozen ties.
All these measures took a hit when Sheikh Hasina was allowed to hold a press conference. India’s foreign ministry distanced itself from the event, with a ministry spokesman saying the government had no role to play in what was an event by a private media entity, and that the government does not endorse anything said at the forum. Even so, especially with regard to the duly constituted government of Bangladesh, the damage was done.
The press event prompted a furious reaction from Dhaka. The government expressed deep outrage and regret, describing the incident as a direct affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh and a grievous insult to the martyrs of the July Revolution. The foreign ministry press note further warned of the severe ramifications such a public platform could have on the reset and restoration of bilateral relations. Bangladesh has already sought Sheikh Hasina’s extradition under the 2013 India-Bangladesh Extradition Treaty.
Hasina’s son Sajeeb Wazed Joy further aggravated the situation by calling Bangladesh a “failed state” and saying it could emerge as a hub for regional terrorism. Speaking virtually from the United States at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club event in New Delhi, he alleged that Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) was operating freely in Bangladesh and accused the current government of allowing the release of hundreds of convicted militants jailed during the Awami League’s rule.
Joy also claimed that banned Islamist organizations such as Hizb ut-Tahrir were now openly holding rallies and that individuals linked to al-Qaida had addressed public gatherings. Describing the situation as a direct security threat to India, he said Bangladesh was becoming “another Pakistan” on India’s eastern frontier, warning that the country’s growing instability would have consequences not only for India but for the wider region.
By giving Sheikh Hasina and her son a platform to lash out at the present regime from Indian soil, India has sent a signal to Dhaka that it still stands with its old friend — Hasina.
Although it goes without saying that India must have calculated the political cost of the event, on the face of it, it looks like India, with one stroke, has brought all efforts to mend ties to naught.
The reason for having friendly ties with the regime is that Bangladesh is India’s second-biggest trading partner in the region and its geographical location is also important for India’s strategic interests.
Speaking to Al Arabiya English, senior analyst Derek Grossman described Sheikh Hasina’s ouster as “a major blow to Indian strategy,” creating a diplomatic irritant and setback for New Delhi’s regional security framework.
This became apparent when Prime Minister Rahman chose China over India for his first foreign visit, where he signed an MoU with China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC), a Chinese state-owned company, to develop the China-Bangladesh Mongla Port Economic Zone. The Chinese proposal is reportedly worth about $650 million and includes attracting Chinese manufacturing, developing bonded warehouses and turning the area into a logistics hub.
The crucial point for India is that this land had originally been earmarked for an Indian economic zone. Mongla itself is Bangladesh’s second-largest seaport, and India has had significant strategic and commercial interest in it as it is strategically located in southwestern Bangladesh, close to the Bay of Bengal and India’s eastern seaboard. According to Bangladeshi sources, 12 Chinese companies have proposed investments totaling $9.21 billion following Rahman’s visit to China.
The second is the newfound bonhomie between Dhaka and Islamabad. Under Hasina, relations with Pakistan were severely constrained by the 1971 Liberation War legacy and war crimes trials of domestic pro-Pakistan actors like Jamaat-e-Islami.
As a result, defense cooperation between Pakistan and Bangladesh has seen a sudden acceleration.
In January 2025, a six-member Bangladeshi military delegation led by Lieutenant General SM Kamrul Hasan visited Pakistan and held meetings with the chiefs of Pakistan’s three armed services.
Then the air chiefs of Bangladesh and Pakistan held talks in Islamabad in January 2026 on possible procurement of Pakistan’s JF-17 Thunder fighter aircraft.
Before giving Hasina the platform, the Indian government should have considered that the present dispensation in Dhaka is antagonistic towards India.
Calling India’s position contradictory, Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said that giving Hasina a political platform and seeking friendly ties cannot go together.
Only time will tell the implications of this fallout, but on the face of it, it looks like a miscalculated move.

articles.title: Southeast Asia’s Border Disputes: Wars in Waiting?
articles.full_text:
The region’s maritime borders are hotly contested, but on land there’s the real risk of conflict, too.
You probably have heard of the South China Sea disputes – a major flashpoint involving China, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, and Brunei. But the South China Sea isn’t the only dispute threatening to spark a war in Southeast Asia. There are plenty more contested borders on land as well.
Today, we’re going to talk about three other territorial disputes in the region – the kind of flashpoints that stay below the headlines until it’s too late. Stay tuned, because we’re ranking them in order: from the least likely to spark an actual shooting war to the highest risk of conflict. 
In fact, one of these disputes even flared into a full-blown shooting war in 2025 – and it could happen again at any time.
